title: 8 Tips from the TS Wizard - using, as const, never
summary: Matt Pocock live-streams a walkthrough of eight advanced TypeScript tips, teaching each from first principles in the TypeScript Playground. He builds a type helper that extracts string-valued keys using a mapped type plus conditional types (returning never for non-matching keys), demonstrates the TS 5.2 fix for array-union method calls like filter and find, shows how indexed access types with number extract a union from an array type, demystifies the empty object type, and introduces the raise-returns-never idiom for early errors. He finishes with the loose-autocomplete trick (union plus string and empty object) and a deep dive into the using declaration from the TC39 explicit resource management proposal, implemented in the TS 5.2 beta via Symbol.dispose and Symbol.asyncDispose. The stream closes with Q&A and a tour of his new shed-quarters streaming setup.
what_you_learn: You learn the mid-to-advanced TypeScript type-level toolbox - mapped types, conditional types, never as a union filter, indexed access types, and as const - explained as composable building blocks rather than magic. For a developer building AI-agent systems, this is exactly the skill set needed to write strongly typed tool APIs, config schemas, and harness code where the compiler, not runtime checks, catches misuse.

skills.name: TypeScript Type System
skills.description: A function annotated to return never, callable inline with nullish coalescing, so invalid states throw early and narrow types.

learnings.title: Wrap gnarly inline types in named type helpers
learnings.detail: Starting from a hard-to-read inline type that extracts string-valued keys, Matt refactors it into ExtractStringKeys as a generic type function with a T parameter, then generalizes it to ExtractKeysWhereValuesAreOfType by making the value type a second generic. The lesson: type functions that call other type functions let a reader understand code top-down - 'gets the values of the object' at the type level - instead of decoding one giant expression.

learnings.title: never removes itself from any union
learnings.detail: Building the key extractor step by step: a mapped type K in keyof Obj returns K where Obj[K] extends string, otherwise never. Mapped over the object this yields e.g. 'id' | 'name' | never, and because never cannot coexist with other union members it disappears, leaving exactly the wanted keys. Matt stresses the mental model: never lives alone, but placed with anything else it vanishes - the core mechanism behind many advanced type tricks.

learnings.title: The impim pattern transforms unions in one expression
learnings.detail: Matt names and demonstrates the 'immediately indexed mapped type' (impim): create a mapped type and immediately index into it with keyof T, which turns the mapped results back into a union. He references his article 'Transform Any Union In TypeScript' and notes the pattern is one of the most generally useful type-level techniques whenever you work with unions.

learnings.title: TS 5.2 fixes array methods on unions of arrays
learnings.detail: In TS 5.1 and earlier, calling .filter or .find on a parameter typed (Fizz | Buzz)[] refactored to a union of arrays Fizz[] | Buzz[] failed with a confusing 'no overload matches this call' error, forcing ugly workarounds like generic function wrappers. Switching the playground to the nightly (5.2 beta), the identical code just works - the release notes call it 'easier method usage for unions of arrays' - and the fix had been requested for years.

learnings.title: Array[number] extracts a union of all array members
learnings.detail: Given const roles = ['user', 'superadmin', 'admin'] as const, typeof roles captures the readonly tuple, and RolesArray[number] indexes into it with the number type to produce 'user' | 'superadmin' | 'admin'. Passing a union of numeric literals (RolesArray[0 | 1 | 2]) also works because indexed access distributes over the union. Matt calls this his favorite trick - people constantly ask how to do it and it appears everywhere in real codebases.

learnings.title: as const is required, and JSON imports lose literal types
learnings.detail: Importing roles from a .json file with resolveJsonModule works, but without as const (which JSON imports do not support - an open TypeScript issue) the array is inferred as plain string, so RolesArray[number] collapses to string. Without as const upstream, TypeScript has no better information to dive deeper into. Unions are also unordered sets - the display order of extracted members is an illusion.

learnings.title: The empty object type means anything but null and undefined
learnings.detail: Counterintuitively, an interface Empty {} accepts '', 0, false, NaN, and any object - every value except null and undefined. The precise mental model (contributed by David Blass in chat): it represents anything where accessing a property will not throw at runtime, since null and undefined are the only values where property access throws. Falsy values like 0 are fine because 0.toFixed exists; null can never hold a property.

learnings.title: Everything type equals empty object or null or undefined, which is unknown
learnings.detail: Matt poses the puzzle of representing every TypeScript type without any and without unknown: the answer is {} | null | undefined. This is exactly how the top type unknown operates under the hood - it accepts everything because it is the union of the property-accessible universe plus the two property-throwing values. Interface Object is different: it is a hook for globally appended attributes, not a type to use.

learnings.title: A raise function returning never enables inline error throwing
learnings.detail: A function const raise = (error: string): never => { throw new Error(error) } never completes, so its return type is never (not void). Used with nullish coalescing - const id = props.params.id ?? raise('ID is required') - it throws in the right branch and narrows id to string afterward, all in one line. Credit to MapleLeaf_ on Twitter for the idiom; Next.js uses the same never-returning pattern for redirect() and notFound() in the app directory.

learnings.title: Loose autocomplete via string and empty object
learnings.detail: If a prop is IconType | string, TypeScript eagerly collapses the union to string and autocomplete is lost. Wrapping it as IconType | (string & {}) keeps the literal members visible in autocomplete while still accepting any string. The extra intersection is a bit of computation that stops eager collapsing; Matt notes the same trick appears in React's own types, and it connects to the empty-object lesson since string already supports property access.

learnings.title: using and await using give deterministic resource disposal
learnings.detail: The TC39 explicit resource management proposal (stage 3, so likely coming to JavaScript) adds using resource = getResource() and await using for async disposal. The initializer must be an object with a [Symbol.dispose] or [Symbol.asyncDispose] method (TypeScript catches misuse), and the resource is disposed automatically when it leaves scope - replacing try/catch/finally boilerplate for things like database connections. A plain block scope disposes early; in the playground it requires target esnext. Analogous to C# using, Java try-with-resources, and Go defer.

key_points: never removes itself from any union - the silent filter behind most type-level tricks.
Array[number] is the idiomatic way to turn a tuple into a union of its members.
An empty object type {} accepts every value except null and undefined.
{} | null | undefined is how unknown works under the hood.
Raise-returning-never plus nullish coalescing throws inline and narrows the type in one line.
Union with string and empty object keeps autocomplete alive while accepting any string.
TS 5.2 finally makes filter and find work on unions of arrays.
as const is what gives TypeScript literal precision - without it upstream types collapse to string.
